title: Evidence-Graded Battery Pilot
problem: Avangrid can't yet fund or file a home battery program, because its value depends on equipment guesses the utility can't check. Half the listed EV homes show no home charging, heat pumps can't be told apart from resistance heat, and the payback runs longer than the battery warranty. A deck that leads with big MW and bill-savings numbers will not get through a regulator or a capital committee. The utility needs to know which battery claims its own meters already prove, and what pilot would prove the rest.
specific_user: The Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage (judge Bruce Balch, per the kickoff deck) works with the Director, Regulatory Affairs NY to take a behind-the-meter battery pilot to the NY PSC and to internal capital approval. Their decision has three parts: which homes go into the first pilot tranche, how many batteries those homes get, and which value claims (peak relief, avoided service upgrade, bill savings) are strong enough to put in the filing and which have to wait for the pilot to measure them.
solution:
Inputs are the pipeline's existing outputs: 4,079 battery candidates, per-home class flags with their confidence, the EV, heat-pump and solar label lists, and the hourly matrix with weather.

Method, in four steps:
(1) For each candidate, simulate dispatch of the 2x IQ 10C unit (7.68 kW, 20.16 kWh, 89.4% round-trip) against the system's top 20 and top 50 hours, the metric Scott asked for. The current number is a single 4-hour event window.
(2) Give every claim about every home an evidence grade. A means checked against Avangrid's own lists (solar: 91.1% recall, 86% precision). B means a strong weather fit (AC, high-confidence electric heat). C means inferred with low confidence (heat pump, EV Level 1).
(3) Backtest a measurement and verification baseline. Predict each candidate's load on the 10 held-out peak days from same-temperature days, and report the measured error at the home level and at the tranche level.
(4) Build pilot tranche 1 from homes where both the peak-relief claim and the 3 kVA electrification claim are grade A or B. For each of those homes, write down the predicted kW on the top hours before any battery is installed.

Output: a ranked CSV with grade and predicted kW per home; a claims ledger slide (claim, number, grade, how it gets verified); and a staged pilot plan. After one summer, the pilot turns the C-grade claims into measured, fileable MW.
class_framework_use:
Zott & Huy (2007) say resource holders fund a new venture on symbols when uncertainty is high and they can't see its real quality (Session 12 brief, ZH pp. 94-97). A utility battery program pitched to the NY PSC fits those conditions exactly: AMI disaggregation is a black box to the regulator, and the economics are unproven.

Rindova et al. (2006) explain why the room will lean on a celebrity example, Green Mountain Power's 5,500-home, ~110 MW Vermont fleet (cited). Celebrity also shields bad news, so decks that copy that story will bury the 23 to 33 year payback.

The Session 12 brief adds the step that changed our problem: a signal that both real and fake ventures can collect moves the odds by zero, and only verification moves them. That turned "rank battery homes" into "make the program's quality visible." We grade the evidence behind each claim, write predictions down before the pilot, and measure them with a backtested baseline. That is the credibility signal a weak program cannot copy. The judges see a sharper problem and a filing-ready pilot, never the class vocabulary.

title: Promise-Graded Battery Offer List
problem: The battery program's most persuasive promises are also its least checked. "Add an EV charger with no service upgrade" rests on hourly averages that make the 3 kVA test optimistic. "$359 a year in savings" rests on assumed tariffs. "A 4.2 kW peak cut" assumes perfect foresight. If those numbers reach offer letters and regulatory filings without labels, Avangrid will promise customers results the meters cannot support and claim megawatts it cannot measure.
specific_user: The Customer Programs and Products Manager (Andrew Leja's role on the judging panel), who decides which homes get a battery, managed-charging or heat-pump offer first and what the offer letter promises. Regulatory Affairs NY reuses the same numbers when it files program MW, so it is the second user.
solution:
The layer sits on the existing pipeline outputs (bess_candidates.csv, customer_classes.csv, facts.json and the assumption.* values). It tags each candidate home's claims (peak cut, bill savings, EV or heat pump enabled without an upgrade, appliance owned) as Measured, Modeled or Assumed, and gives each a range. It then re-tests each claim three ways:
(1) It dispatches the battery on a fixed day-ahead 4-9 pm window instead of perfect foresight, which gives a realistic kW range.
(2) It reruns the 3 kVA headroom test with a safety margin of 0 to 1.5 kW for sub-hourly peaks.
(3) It sweeps tariffs for savings and payback.
Each home lands in one of three lanes. "Offer now" means a measured basis, a high-confidence class, and a 3 kVA pass even with the margin. "Verify first" means a thin margin or a low-confidence class such as heat pump or EV Level 1. Those homes get a 15-minute data pull, or a one-question opt-in to the customer ("Do you charge an EV at home?"), and the answers feed back as training labels. "Do not promise" covers seasonal homes and value that rests only on assumptions. The output is a ranked offer file with allowed claim wording per home, plus a one-slide claims register that gives every program number its basis, its range, and the check that would firm it up.
class_framework_use: Tenbrunsel and Messick (2004) show that wrongdoing usually happens through small re-labelings, not lies. Each step looks like the last, so the moral side fades. Here that slope is visible in our own outputs: "likely EV (list not physically validated)" becomes "EV home", the "perfect foresight" 4.2 kW becomes "4.2 kW reduction", and "ASSUMED rates" becomes "save $359". Zuzul and Mohliver (2026) give the test: a specific claim moving from "can" to "does" before it is verified. So the framework chose the problem, which is uncertainty fading as numbers move from analytics to offers to filings. The fix is to tag each number's basis where it is created, so no later step can quietly re-label it. Morrison (2023) finds that felt impact drives voice, and that "others know it too" suppresses it. Everyone knows hourly data is optimistic, yet nothing stops the 22,346 figure. So the tool makes the caveat structural, and it adds a voice channel (the opt-in question and field-crew corrections) whose answers visibly change the model and the offer.

title: Meter-Picked Battery Offer List
problem: Anyone can sell a home battery, but whether it relieves Avangrid's peak depends on which home it sits in, and only Avangrid's meters can see that. Today that knowledge lives in rebate lists that miss most of what's behind the meter. So a program that enrolls whoever applies, or whoever a vendor sells to, will put incentive dollars into homes whose load isn't there in the few hours the grid is built for.
specific_user: Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage, who is designing the BTM BESS program. The decision: which homes are eligible for the subsidized two-unit IQ 10C setup, and the most the program should pay per home. The Customer Programs & Products Manager uses the same list to run enrollment and vendor outreach.
solution: Inputs are the existing pipeline's hourly load matrix for 25,653 homes, the system load, the per-home coincident-peak columns already in customer_segments.csv, the class flags, and the three rebate lists. Method: (1) score each home by the kW the two-battery setup removes in the system's top 20, 50 and 100 hours (Scott's framing), times how often the home is loaded on event days; (2) tag each home's 3 kVA electrification headroom; (3) run an enrollment counterfactual giving MW per 1,000 batteries under four rules: meter-ranked, highest annual kWh (how a vendor chasing big bills would pick), solar owners first, and random applicants; (4) set a per-home incentive ceiling of relief kW x assumed $/kW-yr x 15-year warranty. Output: a ranked offer list that leaves Avangrid as only customer number, tier, eligibility flag and incentive ceiling. The load data and the model stay in-house, and vendors get an install list. The deck adds one chart comparing MW per 1,000 batteries under the four rules and one table of which candidates no current list knows about.
class_framework_use: From CVD vs A.S. Markham (Session 7): Markham lost because it could not name its supposed secrets, had published them, and fought over what anyone could copy, while ignoring the asset that was really protectable. Applied to Avangrid, the battery hardware and the install are what anyone can copy. The 20.16 kWh Enphase spec is public, and Green Mountain Power runs a similar leased two-battery program. The protectable asset is the hourly meter view of which homes sit at the top system hours. Vendors and customers cannot see it. Like Markham's secrets, though, this knowledge is unnamed today: the rebate lists miss half of what the meters show. So the problem worth solving is to turn that meter knowledge into a named, documented, repeatable list, and to let it, rather than self-selection, decide who gets a battery. From the Gans & Stern (2003) commercialization matrix, covered in the class brief from summaries and not the article: the party holding the asset others cannot copy should keep it and contract for the complementary ones. That is why the list shares eligibility flags with installers and never the load data or the model. Reitzig (2004), also from summaries, says to choose deliberately what to publish and what to keep. That becomes a single slide on what leaves the building and what stays. None of this vocabulary goes on the slides. It shows up as the four-rule counterfactual and the share-or-keep design.

title: Batteries Where Thermostats Cannot Reach
problem: Avangrid's one proven flexibility tool, the summer smart-thermostat event, has no winter version customers will accept, yet electric heat already carries 31.9% of winter peak-hour load and about 5,100 more heat conversions would make this system winter-peaking. A battery program ranked on summer peakiness, as most teams will rank it, spends scarce batteries on hours a cheaper thermostat event already covers and leaves the hard winter evenings with no tool.
specific_user: The Customer Programs and Products Manager, who runs the summer smart-thermostat program and has to decide which homes get the program battery offer and which season each battery is dispatched for. The Director of Advanced Load Forecasting uses the same output to track how close the territory is to a winter peak.
solution: Inputs are the pipeline's per-home summer and winter event-window relief from bess.py, each home's weather-driven AC load and electric-heat flags from classify.py, and the top-N system hours in each season. Method: compute "residual relief", meaning the kW a battery delivers in the top system hours after subtracting what the cheaper tool already sheds (the thermostat share of AC load in summer, an assumed 33% swept from 20 to 50%; nothing in winter, because no accepted winter setback exists). Rank by residual relief across both seasons, plus a flag for electric-heat and EV homes that would otherwise fail the 3 kVA rule. Then backtest old and new rankings on how many of the top 20/50/100 hours each one cuts, the measure Scott named. Output: a ranked candidate CSV with tool assignment (thermostat, battery, or both), a supply curve showing MW per 1,000 batteries in winter and summer under both rankings, and a winter-flip counter that turns each new heat-pump rebate into kW toward the 16.8 MW summer-winter gap.
class_framework_use: Innovator's DNA (Dyer, Gregersen, Christensen, 2009) chose the problem rather than labelling it. Questioning ("question the unquestionable") went after the challenge's own premise that the peakiest summer home is the best battery home, and asked what a battery does that nothing cheaper can. Observing (Scott Cook's "What's different than you expected?") flagged a surprise in our own supply curve: the best 1,000 homes give more winter MW (4.43) than summer MW (2.72), in a system that peaks in summer. Networking came from the judge himself at office hours, where Scott doubted a winter thermostat program would work on a minus-10 degree day. Associating joined that doubt to the surprise and to a cold-climate analogue (Green Mountain Power in Vermont, batteries in 5,500+ homes, about 110 MW, citations.yaml vermont-gmp-vpp): batteries are the winter demand-response tool customers do not have to feel. Experimenting became the backtest on the top hours of each season, so the reframe is tested rather than asserted.

title: One Peak, One Offer Router
problem: Avangrid sizes its grid for the top few system hours, but it reaches homes through separate programs (thermostat DR, EV, heat pump, battery). Each program recruits from its own list, and those lists do not match the meters. The result: the costliest tool, a battery, gets aimed at peak kW that a cheaper lever could remove. Program MW also can't simply be added, because the battery list and the thermostat estimate count much of the same summer AC load.
specific_user: The Customer Programs & Products Manager, the kickoff judge role that owns program design. Each season they decide which homes get which offer: a thermostat setback, managed EV charging, a pool-pump timer, a heat-pump rebate or a program battery. Inputs are the existing pipeline outputs: per-home coincident kW at the summer and winter event hours (customer_segments.csv), the class flags and probabilities (customer_classes.csv), each home's AC weather-driven load at event hours (computed in analysis/bess.py), its Level 2 charging blocks and its battery relief (bess_candidates.csv), plus the 3 kVA headroom test.

Method:
1. For each home and each lever, compute the kW that lever removes during the top 50 system hours of each season, which is Scott's stated objective.
2. Route each home to its cheapest adequate lever first: thermostat setback for summer AC load, managed charging for Level 2 EV blocks, a timer for the pool-pump floor.
3. Give a battery only to the residual. That means peak no cheaper lever reaches (winter electric-heat peaks, where Scott doubts setbacks will be accepted, and flat high load), or homes where a planned EV or heat pump fails the 3 kVA rule without storage.
4. Treat lever cost per kW as an editable parameter with sensitivity bands, not a claimed number.

Outputs:
1. A per-home "next best offer" CSV that every program pulls from, one shared queue in place of separate lists.

class_framework_use:
The Nadler-Tushman congruence model (Hiatt & Weber, 2012, Congruence Model Note) says to name the critical task first and then test whether the formal organization fits it. A part is never judged as good on its own.

1. The critical task. For a T&D utility, Scott names it: cut demand in the top hours, because "the infrastructure is built to meet that" [15:52].
2. The misfit. The formal organization, meaning programs split by technology that each target from their own rebate list, is the poor fit. That is a performance gap, and the data shows it: half the listed EV homes never charge at Level 2 at home, while hundreds of unlisted homes do.
3. Why splitting the work fails. The note's interdependence test says the levers are reciprocal: a thermostat and a battery chase the same AC kW in the same hours. Programs run as pooled, independent units, so their MW gets summed, double counted and spent on the costliest tool.
4. The fix. Keeping Google Googley (Groysberg et al., 2008) shows one formal fix: Google kept a functional structure with no business-unit P&L, which Brian Axe says "prevented business unit fiefdoms." Our equivalent is one shared targeting queue and one metric, dollars per kW cut in the top hours, so each program is judged against the same task.

The framework shows up in the deck as a better question ("which lever per home?" in place of "which homes get a battery?"), not as vocabulary.

problem: If Avangrid judges its 4,079 battery candidates the way it judges demand-response programs, they pay back in 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty, so the battery program fails. The summer-afternoon homes on that list could be served more cheaply by the smart-thermostat program Avangrid already runs. That leaves the winter electric-heat peak and the homes adding Level 2 chargers, the places only a battery can serve, with no ranking.
specific_user: The Customer Programs & Products Manager (a judge's role). This person decides which offer each home gets (summer thermostat event, managed EV charging or a program battery) and which program pays for it. They need one list that puts batteries only where the existing programs cannot reach, so the battery business case holds up when the regulators review it.
solution: The input is the existing pipeline's per-home outputs: AC weather load, EV Level 2 flags, the electric-heat flag, the 3 kVA headroom test and event-hour load, plus the top 50 system hours computed from the summed AMI load. Each home's share of those top hours goes through a waterfall, cheapest program first. Step one is the summer thermostat event, at the assumed 33% cooling shed. Step two is managed charging, which moves Level 2 blocks out of the top hours. Step three is the battery, dispatched at 7.68 kW, 20.16 kWh and 89.4% round trip. The battery covers only what is left: winter electric-heat peaks, flat loads that thermostats miss, and homes that would break the 3 kVA rule when they add a charger or heat pump. The output is a per-home CSV naming the program that owns each home, MW covered at the top summer and winter hours by each program, and a re-run payback for the smaller battery list compared with the 4,079-home list. It ends with a staged pilot: the first battery cohort, a measured-relief milestone, and a rule for handing proven homes to distribution planning as an alternative to a service upgrade.
class_framework_use: Christensen & Overdorf (2000) put the failure point in processes and values rather than resources. Avangrid has the battery hardware and the data, but the yardstick that would rank a battery program is the demand-response cost per peak kW. On that yardstick the battery scores below thermostats (9.9 MW of thermostat relief vs 23 to 33 year battery payback), so the program dies in review. Their rule is to put each opportunity where its processes and values fit. Summer AC relief goes to the thermostat program Avangrid already runs (processes and values both fit). EV flexibility goes to managed charging (light adaptation). Batteries go only to the gaps that existing processes cannot cover: the winter heat peak, where Scott expects customers to resist winter thermostat setbacks, and the 3 kVA service-study trigger. From Chesbrough & Socolof (2000), Lucent's NVG ventures were staged, given milestones and bought back by the core (Elemedia). The battery cohort therefore runs as a staged pilot with a measured-relief milestone and a written handoff rule into distribution planning, not as an open-ended program. The deck shows this as a routing waterfall and a pilot gate, with none of the class vocabulary.

title: Batteries for Jobs Thermostats Can't
problem: Avangrid will judge a home-battery program by the test its existing tool already passes, summer peak MW per dollar and bill payback, and on that test batteries lose: an AC thermostat setback gives about 9.9 MW cheaply while batteries take 23 to 33 years to pay back against a 15-year warranty. That test hides the two jobs only a battery can do: cutting the winter cold-hour peak, where customers are unlikely to accept thermostat setbacks, and letting a home add an EV charger or heat pump without breaking the 3 kVA service rule.
specific_user: The Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage, who has to decide which homes the first behind-the-meter battery program enrolls and what value it claims to regulators. Load Research (Scott, Program Director) supplies the test it is judged on: relief in the system's top hours.
solution: Inputs: hourly AMI for the 25,653 homes, hourly weather, the pipeline's per-home class flags (AC, electric heat, EV Level 2, seasonal), and the challenge's battery spec (2 x IQ 10C, 20.16 kWh, 7.68 kW, 89.4% round-trip). Method: find the system's top 50 hours in each season. Split each home's load in those hours into what the existing summer thermostat program can shed (AC weather-driven load times the assumed shed) and what it cannot (winter heat, EV charging, non-AC load). Then dispatch the battery only against that remainder, charging off-peak, and rerun the 3 kVA test for an added EV or heat pump with 0, 1 or 2 units. Output: a per-home job ledger (thermostat / battery-winter / battery-headroom / neither), top-hour MW by tool and season, a ranked battery list scored on relief no thermostat can give plus service studies avoided, and for each battery home the break-even avoided-upgrade cost. Avangrid checks that last number against its own upgrade costs instead of trusting our assumed prices.
class_framework_use: Morison (1966) shaped the problem first. The Bureau of Ordnance tested continuous-aim firing on solid ground at the Washington Navy Yard and proved it "impossible," because it ran the test in the old method's environment, not at sea where the ship's roll did half the work (Morison 1966, p.64). Avangrid's default battery test, summer MW per dollar plus bill payback, is that solid-ground test: it is the thermostat's home ground, and the pipeline already shows batteries failing it (23 to 33 year payback). So the problem we picked is "which test kills the battery program, and what is the battery's real environment?" The answer is winter top hours and the 200 A service. Morison also shaped the solution. Sims's attacks made surrender look like defeat (p.68), and people defend the devices they built (pp.67-68). So the tool never pitches batteries against the thermostat program. It dispatches the thermostat first in summer and leaves that program's owners unchanged. Batteries start where no incumbent tool exists, which is Morison's Cambria move (pp.67-68): winter, where no thermostat program has launched, and homes adding EV or heat pump load. The frame is the judges' own words, top hours [15:15] and the 3 kVA rule, not class vocabulary.

title: Installed Base Before Batteries
problem: Avangrid's battery shortlist ranks homes only by how peaky they are. It picks 4,079 homes that would need 8,158 batteries ($73-106M, a 23-33 year payback against a 15-year warranty). But 2,582 of those homes are summer air-conditioning peakers, and the summer thermostat program Avangrid already runs could cut that same peak. So the battery money pays for relief that customers' existing equipment can already give, and the list never singles out the homes where only a battery works: winter electric-heat homes and homes about to add a charger or heat pump.
specific_user: The Customer Programs & Products Manager (one of the judges). For the next program cycle, this manager decides which offer each home gets: smart-thermostat enrollment, managed EV charging, a pool-pump timer or the two-unit Enphase battery. The manager also splits the budget between the summer thermostat program and the battery pilot. The Senior Manager for Clean Energy Policy (Energy Storage) uses the same output to decide which homes, and how many, go into a battery filing.
solution: The tool takes the existing pipeline's outputs as inputs: per-home classifications (AC, pool, Level 2 EV, electric heat, water heater), segments, battery tiers and relief, plus hourly load in the summer event window (16:00-20:00 on 2 July) and the winter window (17:00-21:00 on 8 February). For each home it first estimates the kW that equipment the home already owns could shed in those windows. That covers a thermostat setback (33% of weather-driven cooling kW, an assumption), pool-pump kW moved out of the window, and Level 2 charging moved past 21:00. It then recomputes the home's remaining peak. A home is offered a battery only on one of three tests: (a) its remaining peak still clears the current persistence rule (at least 3.5 kW on 9 of 10 event days), (b) it heats with electricity and peaks in winter, where Scott doubts thermostat setbacks will be accepted, or (c) adding an EV or heat pump would break the 3 kVA rule without storage. The output is a per-home "first offer" column and a supply curve (MW against cost) that stacks programs on existing equipment first and batteries last. It shows how many batteries Avangrid actually needs for the same summer and winter MW, and it can be rerun as-is across millions of meters.
class_framework_use: Shapiro & Varian (1999, pp.15-16) sort options by whether they work with what customers already own. Avangrid's thermostat program fits what customers already have; a new battery does not. A battery has to beat each customer's switching cost, here $9-13k per unit (an assumption) and an install. That fits only where no existing option can do the job. Their CBS-versus-RCA color TV story is this problem in miniature: CBS had the regulator's approval but could not play the shows people already watched, so the system that worked with existing sets won. Here, the 2,582 summer AC peakers can be served through equipment that is already installed. The winter electric-heat homes and the homes adding chargers have no existing option that can flex, and that is where a battery is worth its cost. Cusumano et al. (1992), VHS over Beta: Sony lost with a better product because it would not let other firms build Betamax machines. That points to the roadmap: enroll customer-owned thermostats, chargers and batteries of any brand instead of relying on one vendor. The brief's stress test sets the limit: opening up a program works only when it attaches to a network big enough to join. Avangrid's AMI meters on every home and its existing thermostat program are that network, which is why the existing-equipment programs come first in the stack.

title: Batteries Where Thermostats Cannot Reach
problem: The usual pitch for a utility home battery program, peak shaving plus bill savings, fails on Avangrid's own numbers. Batteries at the 4,079 persistent-peak homes cost $73-106M and pay back in 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty (assumed prices), and a summer thermostat setback buys 9.9 MW without any hardware. The person who has to win funding for a battery program has no case unless candidates are chosen for value that only a battery delivers: the winter peak, where customers will not accept a thermostat setback, and the service upgrade a battery avoids.
specific_user: The Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage, who must take a behind-the-meter battery program to Avangrid's capital approvers and, with Regulatory Affairs NY, to the NY regulator. The decision is which homes get batteries in the first tranche and which value case to file. The Customer Programs & Products Manager uses the same list to choose which homes go to thermostat DR instead.
solution: Inputs are the existing pipeline outputs: hourly load for 25,653 homes, weather, the class flags (electric heat, EV L2/L1, heat pump, emerging segment), the battery dispatch from bess.py and the 3 kVA headroom test. Method, step 1: rank the system's top 50 summer and top 50 winter hours, which Scott says the grid is built for, and compute how many kW each home's two-unit battery delivers in each of those hours. Step 2: tag each home with the cheapest tool that covers its peak. Summer, AC-driven homes go to thermostat DR. Winter electric-heat homes (17:00-21:00, the 2.1F peak) go to batteries, because Scott doubts a winter thermostat setback will be accepted. Homes likely to add a Level 2 charger or heat pump that fail the 3 kVA rule without a battery are tagged upgrade-avoidance. Step 3: for each battery home, compute the break-even avoided-upgrade value, the dollar amount that brings payback inside the 15-year warranty, so Avangrid can enter its own upgrade cost and see the list re-sort. Outputs are a ranked CSV with a case label, confidence and break-even per home, a portfolio chart of MW against dollars for thermostats and batteries by season, and a one-page case card per top home that plots its own load on 2 July and 8 February with the battery covering the peak.
class_framework_use: Conger (1998) supplied the problem, not the wording. His step 2 says that when no shared gain exists, you change the plan rather than the pitch, like the jet-engine manager who rebuilt his proposal from 'speed' to 'profit'. The pipeline's own payback (23-33 yr vs 15-yr warranty) shows a peak-shaving battery program has no shared gain with a cost-focused approver. So the problem became finding the homes where a battery delivers value the approver already counts: avoided upgrades and the winter top hours. The Session 8 brief's Ruffo test (a frame persuades only if it is true from the audience's side) becomes the break-even calculation, which the user fills with Avangrid's own upgrade cost instead of trusting ours. Step 1, credibility, became a confidence tag on each claim, checked against Avangrid's own lists: solar is strong (91.1% recall) and heat pumps are weak (AUC 0.718), stated openly. Step 3, vivid evidence, became a per-home trace on the actual peak days instead of an aggregate MW figure. Step 4, emotional match, came from Scott's own worry about asking customers to set back heat on a -10F day, so the battery is positioned as the winter tool that leaves the thermostat alone. Pfeffer (1992), from the same session, informed who the user is: the champion needs the regulatory approver's frame, not the analyst's.

title: Batteries for the Next Peak
problem: Avangrid would rank 15-year battery sites on one year of meter data, and that year peaks on summer air conditioning. Home electrification is about to move the system peak to winter: about 5,100 more electric-heat conversions flip it. A ranking built on today's summer peak puts batteries where smart thermostats already cover the load and misses the cold-evening peak that thermostats cannot reach.
specific_user: The Senior Manager of Clean Energy Policy for Energy Storage, who owns the BTM BESS program (a judge's role). This manager decides which homes get a two-unit IQ 10C system under a 15-year warranty. The Director of Advanced Load Forecasting supplies the adoption scenario and owns the annual re-check.
solution: Inputs are the pipeline's per-home summer and winter relief from two batteries (bess_candidates.csv), its class flags and probabilities, its 3 kVA headroom test, and the hourly system load. Step one rebuilds the system load under a sweep of 0 to 10,000 electric-heat conversions, adding 3.29 kW per home at the winter peak, and finds which season binds and which top-50 hours set the peak in each scenario. Step two scores every home on battery relief in the binding top hours, minus what the summer thermostat program already sheds, plus credit for adding an EV or heat pump with no service upgrade. Step three keeps each home's worst-case score across the scenarios. The output is a ranked list tagged three ways: pays in both seasons, summer-only (leave to thermostats), and electrification enabler. title: Battery Program the Regulator Funds
problem: Avangrid can only run a battery program that the New York regulator approves and ratepayers pay for. On the pipeline's own numbers, batteries used to shave summer peaks take 23 to 33 years to pay back against a 15-year warranty, and they lose to the thermostat program Avangrid already runs. So a list of the "peakiest homes" is a list nobody will fund.
specific_user: The Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage (a judge), working with the Director, Regulatory Affairs NY. They decide which homes, and which justification, go into a behind-the-meter storage program proposal that has to pass the regulator's benefit-cost review. Their question is: "Where does a battery buy something ratepayers would otherwise pay for, and what will that cost per kW at the top system hours?"
solution: The build is a funding-gate layer on the existing pipeline. Its inputs are bess_candidates.csv, customer_classes.csv, the segments, the hourly system load, and one editable assumptions file (capacity $/kW-yr, installed unit cost, thermostat shed, and avoided service or transformer upgrade $ per home). It works in three steps. (1) Find the system's top 20, 50 and 100 hours, which is Scott's stated objective, and give each home a loading order. The thermostat goes first wherever the home's top-hour load is driven by AC. A battery goes only to the remainder: winter top hours, where Scott expects a winter thermostat setback to struggle, and homes where an EV Level 2 charger or a heat pump would break the 3 kVA rule. (2) For each battery home, split the value by who receives it: ratepayers get the top-hour capacity relief and the avoided upgrade, while the participant gets the bill savings. The tool then computes a 15-year ratepayer benefit-cost ratio. (3) Rather than claim a value no team can source, the tool solves for the break-even avoided-upgrade cost per home in each lane. As an illustration, derived from facts.json at the low capex: an avoided upgrade worth about $12k per home lets the full 4,079-home set pass on ratepayer value alone. The output is a three-lane list (thermostat first; battery in the electrification lane; battery in the winter lane) and one slide. That slide shows MW at the top-N hours per $M for each lane, next to the single number the filing must source.
class_framework_use: Christensen & Bower (1996) argue that a firm's freedom to choose its strategy is limited by whoever supplies its resources. Projects that no resource-supplying customer wants "languish for lack of impetus and resources." Seagate built working 3.5-inch drives and cancelled them because its paying customers did not want them. A regulated wires utility gets its resources from the regulator acting for ratepayers, so a battery ranked on peakiness is Seagate's 3.5-inch program: technically sound, with no funder. That changed both the problem and the solution. The ranking target moves from "most peak shaved" to "cost ratepayers avoid." Batteries are aimed where the funder already wants something, namely the state's push on flexibility and electrification (Scott, 07:13) and infrastructure sized to the top hours (15:52). The session's sharpened rule, from the Session 6 brief and the Prairietek vs Conner disk drive cases, is that a newcomer wins only where the incumbent's customers do not already want the incumbent's product. Here the incumbent is the summer thermostat program, which already has regulator approval and delivers 9.9 MW cheaper. The battery is placed only where the thermostat cannot reach: winter hours and electrification upgrades.

title: Smallest Fix That Passes 3 kVA
problem: When a home adds a Level 2 charger, Avangrid's only tools today are a service study or the program's full two-battery setup. That setup pays back in 23 to 33 years on assumed prices, against a 15-year warranty. Most homes need far less to stay inside the 3 kVA rule, so a one-size battery program spends too much per home and reaches too few of the homes that are about to electrify.
specific_user: The Customer Programs & Products Manager (a judge's role) who designs the battery and EV make-ready offers. The decision comes each time a customer asks to add a Level 2 charger or heat pump on a 200 A service: offer a managed-charging schedule, one IQ 10C, the two-unit setup, or send the home to a service study. The Energy Storage policy manager uses the same output to decide how many batteries to request in the program filing and which homes they should go to.
solution: Input: the pipeline's hourly load matrix (25,653 homes x 8,760 h), its 3 kVA test (new peak no more than old peak + 3 kW), the 7.2 kW Level 2 and fitted heat-pump add-on loads, and each home's coincident relief at the summer and winter event hours. Method: for every home, test the add-on load against a ladder of fixes from cheapest to most expensive. Rung 0 is no action. Rung 1 is managed charging: the same nightly kWh delivered only in hours with headroom, which is a new scenario added to passes() in bess.py. Rung 2 is one IQ 10C, rung 3 is two units, and rung 4 is a service study. The tool assigns the lowest rung that passes. It also adds a second unit for peak relief only where that unit's extra coincident kW clears a set cutoff (the median gain is 1.8 kW). Winter electric-heat peakers keep two units, because a thermostat setback cannot reach them. Output: a per-home CSV and Excel lookup (customer number, rung, battery units, kW relief), a count of homes on each rung, and a cost curve comparing the ladder with blanket two-unit deployment. Every dollar figure carries its assumption label.
class_framework_use: The team took the problem from Christensen's question of whether a product oversupplies the job, not from "who is peakiest" (Christensen, 1997, Innovator's Dilemma ch.1). Christensen's disruptors were "technologically straightforward, consisting of off-the-shelf components" and "offered less of what customers in established markets wanted." The two-unit 20.16 kWh setup is the high-end product. For the most common new job, adding an EV without a service upgrade, it oversupplies: one unit already passes 56.6% of homes, and the charger's own scheduling is a simpler, good-enough fix that costs almost no hardware. The Advion lesson in the Session 6 brief is that a technology is sustaining or disruptive relative to a market, not by itself. Here the battery is the right tool for winter electric-heat peakers, which thermostats cannot reach, and too much for EV enablement. Christensen and Bower (1996) explain why the cheap rung gets skipped: resource allocation follows the largest, most demanding projects. The ladder therefore makes the low rung an explicit, counted program option. The class vocabulary never appears in the deck. What the judges see is "more electrified homes per battery dollar."

title: Bridge the Lists, Target Batteries
solution: The tool takes four inputs: the hourly AMI and weather data, the per-home output of the existing pipeline (customer_classes.csv, segments, bess_candidates.csv), the three program lists (EV, heat pump, solar), and the 3 kVA rule with the IQ 10C spec. For each home and each technology, a reconciliation step sorts the meter evidence against the list into one of four states: listed and seen, listed but not seen, seen but not listed, or neither. The pipeline already counts these states. Next the tool works out the home's most likely next load: a Level 2 charger for homes with no EV, or a heat pump for emerging and electric-heat homes. It then tests whether that load stays within 3 kVA with 0, 1 or 2 IQ 10C units and sizes the home at the fewest units that pass, instead of giving all 4,079 candidates two units as the current pipeline does. Each home is then ranked on two measures: coincident relief across the system's top-100 hours (what Scott asked for) and whether the battery replaces a service study. The output is one ranked offer list for the program and storage owners, with a unit count and the reason for each home. Two short exception queues go alongside it: unlisted Level 2 chargers to distribution planning for transformer checks, and listed homes the meters do not confirm to Load Research for list cleanup. Each queue is a simple file of three fields per home, because simple coded facts cross team boundaries and rich analysis does not.
class_framework_use: Fleming & Marx (2006) find that dense, insular clusters are good at developing ideas they already hold but rarely produce a new one, and that new ideas come from the ties that bridge clusters. Inside Avangrid, Load Research, Customer Programs, Energy Storage and Distribution each work like a cohesive cluster with its own list and its own goal. Peak-only battery targeting is the idea each cluster can develop alone. The idea that pays (put the battery where it lets a home add an EV or heat pump without a service upgrade) only appears where the meter, the rebate list, the 3 kVA rule and the battery spec meet. Uzzi & Dunlap (2005) explain why the lists are wrong: the meter is private information that the lists lack, and the disagreement between them is the discrepant information that a closed group never sees. The DOE AMI report confirms that customers rarely tell the utility about a new EV. Fleming & Marx also note that only simple, codified knowledge travels across a network, and that a gatekeeper who alone understands an idea cannot hand it off. That finding shapes the output: no dashboard for one analyst, but per-home files of three fields, each sent to the team that acts on it. In the deck the framework shows up only as the problem choice (one join across four teams' data) and the hand-off design, never as vocabulary.

title: Cheapest Fix Before the Battery
problem: Avangrid's battery program puts the same two-battery setup in every candidate home and justifies it with peak relief and bill savings, which on the pipeline's assumed prices pays back in 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty, while smart thermostats cut the peak more cheaply. The battery's one job that nothing cheaper can do is letting a home add a Level 2 charger without breaking the 3 kVA service rule (99.3% of homes fail without it), and the program has no per-home test showing which homes need two units, which need one, and which need no battery at all.
specific_user: The Customer Programs & Products Manager who designs the battery, EV and heat-pump offers. When the meters show a new Level 2 charger, or a home asks to electrify, that manager has to choose the offer for that home: a charging schedule, one IQ 10C, the two-unit setup, or a referral to engineering for a service study. They also have to tell the energy-storage policy team and regulators what each option costs and how much it cuts the top system hours.
solution: The tool takes the pipeline's 25,653 hourly load profiles (8,760 hours each), the weather file, the existing class flags (Level 2 EV, electric heat, seasonal homes excluded), the challenge's battery spec and 3 kVA rule, and the system's top 20, 50 and 100 hours as Scott described them. For each home and each planned addition (an unmanaged 7.2 kW Level 2 charger, or a heat pump modelled as k x (60F - T)), it tests a ladder of fixes from cheapest to most expensive using the existing passes() check in bess.py. The rungs run as-is, then charging moved into the home's lowest-load hours, then a capped charger, then one IQ 10C, then two units, and finally a service study. The home is assigned the first rung that passes. For that rung the tool also records the kW the home still adds, or removes, in the top system hours. The output is a ranked CSV per home and a program table that sets the flat two-unit design beside the ladder: units bought, capex (on the labelled assumption prices), top-hour MW, and the break-even avoided-upgrade cost per home at which the battery pays back inside its 15-year warranty.
class_framework_use: This comes from the NBA 6650 in-class Systematic Inventive Thinking exercise (Sine, Fall 2026, the fridge redesign). That exercise changes a product using only parts it already has: remove one, copy one, split one, give one a new job, or make one depend on a condition. Here the product is Avangrid's battery program, and its parts are the two IQ 10C units, the 3 kVA rule, the charger schedule and the meter. Removing the second unit, and then the battery itself, showed that one unit closes 56.6% of the Level 2 gaps, and that heat pumps need no battery at 96.8% of homes, so the battery belongs with the EV charger and not the heat pump. Giving the battery a new job, standing in for the service upgrade that the 3 kVA rule would otherwise trigger, gives it a value that thermostats cannot match. That matters because on peak relief alone, 9.9 MW from thermostats undercuts it. Making unit count depend on each home's measured headroom gap replaces "two units for everyone." Splitting EV charging across the 24 hours puts a no-hardware rung ahead of any battery, which follows Scott's point that EVs are the most flexible load. The deck shows these steps as a ladder of fixes per home and never uses the vocabulary.

title: Stage-Gated Battery Pilot Charter
problem: If Avangrid judges a home-battery program by its cost per peak kW, it loses to thermostats: on the pipeline's assumed prices it pays back in 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty. The value only a battery delivers sits in no one's ledger: letting a home add an EV or heat pump without a service upgrade, and cutting winter peak where thermostat setbacks will not be accepted. So the pilot is either killed after year one or sent to the peakiest summer homes, where a thermostat would do the job for less.

Algar Ventures (2021) and Chesbrough and Socolof (2000) show that shared funding and an outside price keep a venture alive when one budget line would kill it, which becomes the customer co-pay lease test. title: Electrify Without a Service Upgrade
problem: Almost every home that adds a Level 2 EV charger breaks the 3 kVA rule, and many add chargers without telling Avangrid, so the cost of service upgrades lands on the utility with no warning. The obvious battery plan, which ranks homes by how peaky their load is, buys peak relief that cheaper thermostat programs already deliver, while each battery takes decades to pay back. Nothing decides, home by home, whether a new load needs no fix, managed charging, a battery, or a real upgrade.
specific_user: The Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage (a judge's role), who runs the program battery and has to defend each placement to NY regulators. The decision comes when a home applies for an EV or heat pump rebate, or is flagged as having added one without telling the utility. That home then gets one of five answers: approve as-is, approve with a capped overnight charger, give it one IQ 10C, give it the two-unit program battery, or send it to engineering for an upgrade study.
solution: The tool takes each home's 8,760 hourly AMI readings, the weather, the rebate lists (EV, heat pump, PV) and a proposed new load: a 7.2 kW Level 2 charger, or a heat pump modeled at 0.051 kW per degree F below 60F. For each home it measures headroom against the 3 kVA rule at that home's own peak hours and at the system's top hours. It then tries the fixes from cheapest to most expensive: none, a charger capped at about 3 kW and moved overnight, one IQ 10C, two units (7.68 kW, 20.16 kWh, 89.4% round trip). Each battery is dispatched hour by hour against the home's own load. The output is a ranked CSV with one verdict per home. It also gives a watch list of homes the meters show already charging at Level 2 without being on the list, checked against their headroom, plus a battery ranking scored on avoided upgrade plus relief in the top 50 system hours. The avoided-upgrade cost per home is an input Avangrid fills from its own upgrade records, never a number we invent.
class_framework_use: Teece (1986), taught through EMI and the CT Scanner (Bartlett, 1983), says that when the core technology is easy to copy, the money goes to whoever owns the complementary assets. EMI's scanner drew "more than a dozen new entrants in the past two years" while EMI was running a three-person sales force and a two-person service team (EMI B). Applied here, the battery is a commodity Enphase product, and a classifier that ranks peaky load is something every team, and every vendor, can build. Bill savings ($359 a year per home) go to whoever sells the battery. Only Avangrid owns four things: every home's meter history from before and after adoption, the rebate lists, the 3 kVA engineering rule, and the cost of service upgrades it must pay. So we dropped the peakiness ranking, which is easy to copy, pays back in 23 to 33 years on assumed prices and loses to thermostats on cost. We chose the problem only those assets can solve: matching each electrification request to the cheapest fix before Avangrid pays for an upgrade. The deck never names Teece. The framework shows up as the value-capture slide: who keeps the bill savings and who keeps the avoided upgrade.

title: Proven Lane, Pilot Lane Router
problem: Avangrid is about to judge a home-battery program on the yardstick it uses for its mature summer thermostat program (dollars per peak kW and payback). On that yardstick batteries lose: a 23 to 33 year payback against a 15-year warranty. That buries the one job batteries do better than anything else in this data, letting a home add an EV charger or heat pump without a service upgrade. It also leaves the winter peak, where Scott doubts thermostat setbacks will work, with no tool.
specific_user: The Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage, who has to propose the BTM battery program to leadership and the NY regulator. That person decides which homes get the first battery units and what the pilot must prove before it earns more money. Second user: the Customer Programs and Products Manager, who decides which homes to enroll in the existing summer smart-thermostat program and in managed EV charging, so the two programs stop competing for the same homes.
solution: Inputs are the pipeline's per-home classes and segments, the hourly loads, the 3 kVA headroom test and the system's top load hours. Step one routes every home into one of three lanes. Proven lane: summer AC peakers go to thermostat DR and EV homes to managed charging, both judged on $/kW as today. Pilot lane: homes where an added Level 2 charger or heat pump breaks 3 kVA and a battery fixes it, plus electric-heat homes that carry the winter top hours. Hold lane: seasonal and inactive homes. Step two simulates the 2x IQ 10C setup (7.68 kW, 20.16 kWh, 89.4% round trip) on each Pilot home against the system's top 50 hours, which is Scott's metric. It counts the hours covered and the kW cut, and picks 1 or 2 units from the 3 kVA result. Step three swaps the payback for a three-gate scorecard. Gate 1 comes from the meters today: homes enabled and top-hour kW. Gate 2 comes from a pilot of about 100 homes: measured top-hour cut and service upgrades avoided. Gate 3 is the avoided-upgrade cost per home at which the battery breaks even. Derived from facts.json assumption prices, that is about $6k to $14k: $18k to $26k capex per home against about $777 a year of bill and capacity value over 15 years. Transformer data must confirm it before the program scales. Output: a ranked CSV for each lane, one slide for each lane and the gate scorecard.
class_framework_use: Govindarajan and Sebell (2012) say incremental innovation runs bottom-up on familiar metrics like Stage-Gate and NPV. A breakthrough needs criteria that move from "educated gut" to familiar metrics only by implementation, and forcing an NPV on a "beginning" idea produces "Imaginary Numbers." That told us where the problem is. Summer thermostat DR is Avangrid's incremental machine, run "for years" [07:30], so judging it on $/kW is right. Batteries as an electrification enabler have no benchmark, and the 23 to 33 year payback rests entirely on placeholder prices, which makes it an imaginary number. If the program is pushed through the thermostat yardstick, it gets "bazooka'd." So the solution runs two lanes in parallel, each with its own scorecard. The H&B/MAB case is the warning: an expansion sold to the board as "ours for the taking" and then judged quarter by quarter. A battery program sold on a payback would go the same way. Corning (p.7) supplies the gate design: "pace ourselves and to be certain before we move to the next stage, as each stage gets increasingly expensive." Corning (p.7) also calls its keystone components "system enablers for customers," which is the job the battery does here. Judges see none of this vocabulary. They see two lanes, two scorecards and three gates.

title: Value Batteries on Winter's Curve
problem: Avangrid's battery case is scored against the summer afternoon peak, where smart thermostats already shed air-conditioning load cheaply, so batteries show a 23 to 33 year payback on a 15-year warranty and look like a money pit. The peak that grows with every heating conversion is the winter evening peak, where thermostat setbacks will struggle. The current ranking weighs both seasons the same, so it sends the first batteries to summer air-conditioning homes that a thermostat could serve.
specific_user: Senior Manager, Clean Energy Policy - Energy Storage (a judge), who has to defend a behind-the-meter battery program's benefit-cost case to NY regulators and internal finance. The decision: which homes get the first battery wave, and which peak the program's value is measured against. The secondary user is the Director of Advanced Load Forecasting, who decides when planning has to treat the territory as winter-peaking.
solution: Inputs: the existing pipeline's hourly matrix (25,653 homes x 8,760 hours), weather, class flags and bess_candidates.csv. Step 1 splits each candidate's two-unit battery relief into summer and winter event-hour kW and subtracts what a thermostat could already shed: about 0.5 kW per AC home in summer, and zero in winter by default, adjustable with a slider. What remains is "battery-only kW". Step 2 is a crossover model: winter system peak = 42.6 MW + 3.29 kW x heating conversions, plotted against the 59.4 MW summer peak. It returns the conversion count at which the system flips (about 5,100 homes, 19.9%), recomputed whenever the AMI rules flag new electric-heat homes. Step 3 re-ranks candidates by battery-only kW, weighting each season by how close the system sits to the crossover. The output is a ranked list with a season tag, a two-curve crossover chart, and a program rule: batteries go first to electrified peakers (T1), and summer AC peakers (T3) get thermostats first.
class_framework_use: Schilling & Esmundo (2009) found that solar looked overfunded and flat because they plotted it against the wrong effort axis (government R&D), while its real steep curve ran on manufacturing scale. The Session 2 rule follows from that: know which curve you compete on before Finance judges the slope. Here the battery is being scored on the summer AC peak. That is a mature curve where the dominant design, summer thermostat DR, already wins on cost: Avangrid has run it "for years", and SCE gets 37 MW per event from it (citation doe-sce-thermostat). On that axis batteries look like a money pit. The curve that is steepening is winter peak plotted against heating conversions. Each conversion adds 3.29 kW at the winter peak and almost nothing in summer, and Scott expects thermostats to hit a ceiling on the coldest days. On this axis the battery faces no cheaper rival. The lens changes the decision itself, not only the wording: T1 electrified peakers move ahead of T3 AC peakers, and the benefit-cost case uses winter MW. The deck never says "S-curve". It shows two lines and a crossover point.

title: One-Ledger Battery Case
problem: Judged on any one department's numbers, the behind-the-meter battery fails: peak relief plus bill savings pay it back in 23 to 33 years, and the warranty runs 15. Its biggest value is letting a home add an EV charger or heat pump without a service upgrade, and that value sits in other departments' budgets and decisions, so no single owner sees the full value or picks the homes on it.
specific_user: The Senior Manager of Clean Energy Policy for Energy Storage, who designs the BTM BESS program and must take a case to NY regulators. That person decides which homes get the offer, at what size (1 or 2 IQ 10C units), and which value streams the filing claims. Today the inputs come from three other places, each with its own measure. Load Research owns the candidate lists, Customer Programs owns EV and heat-pump adoption, and Distribution Engineering owns the 3 kVA and service-upgrade decision.
solution: The ledger adds one table to the existing pipeline, reading customer_classes.csv (p_ev, p_heat_pump, end-use flags), customer_segments.csv, bess_candidates.csv and the per-home 3 kVA headroom test in bess.py. Each home gets one row in dollars, with a column for each function and a label naming the owner. Forecasting's column is relief in the system's top event hours times capacity value. Customer Programs' column is TOU bill savings. Distribution's column is whether the home fails the 3 kVA rule for a Level 2 charger or heat pump alone and passes it with 1 or 2 units, weighted by the home's adoption probability. The last column is the break-even: the avoided service-upgrade value per home that makes the battery pay inside its 15-year warranty, computed as installed cost minus 15 years of capacity and bill value. On the pipeline's numbers that is about $6,400 per home at low cost and $14,400 at high cost. The battery is sized by the job it does, so one unit goes where it is enough to pass the electrification test (56.6% of homes) and two go only where grid relief needs them. Each home is then sent to the cheapest tool that does its job. Summer AC peakers with no electrification need go to thermostat DR, EV homes go to managed charging, seasonal homes are excluded, and batteries go to homes that are both peaky and close to electrifying. The output is a ranked candidate CSV plus one deck page. It shows MW and cost per tool, and the three open inputs Avangrid must supply (service-upgrade cost, NYSEG/RG&E tariff, avoided T&D/ICAP value), each with the function that owns it.
class_framework_use: Clark & Wheelwright (1992) show that in a functional structure, work goes "over the wall" and any problem between two functions has no owner. Their Team A/B supercontroller case makes it concrete. With identical structures, Fred treated the vendor delay as the team's problem and saved 11 weeks, while Jim treated it as engineering's problem and saved none. That lens changed which problem we chose. The usual question is "which homes rank highest on a weighted score?" (a team asked Scott exactly that at [14:07]). We asked instead why the battery looks like a losing program. The answer is that its value is split across functions: storage policy sees a 23 to 33-year payback, while the electrification value sits with Distribution Engineering and Customer Programs. The heavyweight team's contract book becomes the deliverable, one ledger every function can sign, with each department's value in the same dollar unit. That also resolves the weighting question by converting units rather than picking weights. Ancona & Caldwell (1991) found that only the "comprehensive" strategy did well at both time points, built on targeted ambassador and task-coordinator work. General scouting hurt performance. So the deck does not end with a wish list of more data. It names three specific inputs and the function that owns each one. Judges never see the jargon, only a ledger with owners and a break-even they can check.

solution: Inputs are the existing pipeline outputs (bess_candidates.csv, customer_classes.csv, the 25,653 x 8,760 load matrix and hourly weather). For each candidate home the tool runs four tests, each written in the language of the person who signs it off. Load Research and Forecasting: kW the 20.16 kWh / 7.68 kW setup delivers across the system's top-100 hours in each season, which is Scott's stated test. Customer Programs: relief left after a 33% thermostat setback (the assumption already in facts.json), so AC-only summer homes go to the thermostat program and only the remainder goes to batteries. Reliability and distribution: would the home break the 3 kVA rule if it added a Level 2 charger or a heat pump, so that the battery stands in for a service study. Regulatory and finance: the break-even avoided-upgrade cost per home that clears the 15-year warranty, about $6.4k to $14.4k. That figure is derived from facts.json as capex minus 15 years of bill and capacity value, and it rests on the assumed prices. The output is a home-by-owner yes/no matrix, a pilot list of the homes that clear every owner's test, and one deck slide per owner showing their own number.
class_framework_use: Pfeffer (1992) says a correct decision changes nothing and the work is implementation, and his seven steps run goal, then who you depend on, their view, their power, then the tactic. Running those steps on a battery program turned the problem from "rank the peakiest homes" into "show each approver the job only a battery does". Morison's Gunfire at Sea (1966) also shaped it. The Bureau defended gear it had built and proved its point with a test on solid ground. Avangrid's equivalent is its own summer thermostat program, and judging batteries on bill-plus-capacity value is a test they are certain to lose. So the tool routes summer AC homes to thermostats instead of attacking that program. Lyons at GE (Championing Wind Energy at GE, 2014) won by building a coalition and holding a ready plan when the dominant business faltered, framed in GE's own terms (Conger, 1998). That points the pilot at the two places thermostats fall short. The first is winter peak relief, where Scott expects setback to struggle. The second is electrification headroom, a pilot on new load where no incumbent tool exists (Morison's Cambria move). The deck uses none of this vocabulary; it shows up as one slide per approver.

build_plan_24h: Hours 0-8. Person A extends analysis/bess.py: finds the system's top-100 hours per season, runs dispatch for each candidate on those hours, and computes battery relief left after the thermostat shed. Person B adds the electrification test (3 kVA with L2 or HP, with and without the battery) and the break-even avoided-upgrade cost per home, writing everything to facts.json with its assumption tags. Person C builds the deck skeleton: problem, the who-must-say-yes map, one slide per approver, pilot list, method and assumptions, and NET line. Hours 8-16. Join the four tests into an owner-by-home matrix and a pilot CSV, render the charts (top-hour coverage by season, thermostat-vs-battery routing, headroom bars), and fill the slides from facts.json only. Hour 16 is the feature freeze. Hours 16-24: run make check so every number traces, then a blind-judge pass against the rubric, fixes, the README section and rehearsal. Cut order if behind: break-even slide detail first, then per-season dispatch (keep summer only), then the routing chart. The matrix and pilot list are never cut.
biggest_risk: Judges score 35% on analytics, and a stakeholder-shaped deck can read as politics rather than modeling. The core dollar figure, the avoided service-upgrade cost, has no sourced value and rests on assumed capex, rate and capacity prices. Mitigation: present it as a break-even threshold the utility fills in, not a claim, and make the four tests visibly quantitative (top-hour kW, kVA, kW after thermostat). A second risk is that perfect-foresight dispatch overstates relief, so the method slide must disclose it.

blockers: Soft: the reliability column barely sorts homes. Existing facts show the 7.2 kW Level 2 EV fails the 3 kVA rule for 99.3% of homes without a battery and passes for 100% with the two-unit setup. Heat pumps pass for 96.8% with no battery. Among the 4,079 candidates this test will read nearly all-yes or all-no, so the home-by-owner matrix partly collapses unless the test changes, for example to one unit only, managed charging, or the margin each home has left.

Soft: 'top-100 hours is Scott's stated test' is not in the source. The office-hours transcript (sources/qa/office-hours-2026-11-12-scott.txt) has Scott on peaky shapes, the coldest and warmest days and hours, NYISO system peaks (July 2 and Feb 7), and the summer thermostat program. It never names a top-100-hours test. The slide has to reword it as our reading of his advice, or a sourcing check or a judge who was in the room will catch it.

Soft: no deck or pptx pipeline exists yet. The current outputs are readout.html and readout.txt. The approver slides, the routing chart and the headroom bars are all new work. checks/check_all.py --deck can already trace the numbers once a deck exists.

Data gap, not a blocker: there is no tariff, upgrade-cost or program-cost data. The $6.4k to $14.4k break-even depends entirely on assumption.* values ($9k to $13k per unit, $100/kW-yr, $0.30/$0.18 TOU), so it can only be shown as a threshold the utility fills in, which the proposal already plans to do.
feas.fallback: Ship two of the four owner tests, both built on code that already exists in analysis/bess.py. The first is top-hour kW: change the event windows in coincident() from 10 days x 4 hours to the system's top 100 hours, summer first (about 2 h). The second is thermostat routing: ac_kw is already computed per AC home, so subtract 33% of it from each candidate's summer relief and send homes whose remainder falls below a threshold to the thermostat program (about 1.5 h). Show the break-even avoided-upgrade cost as one formula line on the method slide, not a per-home slide (about 1 h). For reliability, report the existing pass/fail numbers (0.7% without a battery, 56.6% with one unit, 100% with two) as a single system-level fact instead of a matrix column. The pilot list is the candidates that pass both tests, written to a CSV with the owner columns. The deck is 6 slides built only from facts.json and run through make check. That is about 12 to 14 person-hours, and the matrix and pilot list stay in.
